hints: Remember sodium metal is very reactive and will replace the H in any O-H group, not just in acids. Look carefully at the structure for all of them.
Count how many -CO2H groups plus how many alcohol -OH groups are present in one molecule of citric acid to get the total moles of acidic H.
Use the rule that 2 moles of O-H protons give 1 mole of H2, so halve your total count of O-H groups to find the moles of hydrogen gas.
walkthrough:
**Spot all the groups that react with sodium**

Sodium reacts with any labile proton on oxygen. That means both carboxylic acids and alcohols react.

$$2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_2$$

**Count the O-H groups in citric acid**

Look at the displayed structure. There are three $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ groups and one tertiary alcohol $\text{HO-C}$ group.

Total reactive H per molecule = 3 + 1 = 4

**Convert moles of H to moles of H2**

From the equation, 2 moles of O-H give 1 mole of $\text{H}_2$. So 1 mole of H gives 0.5 mole of $\text{H}_2$.

$$\text{moles H}_2 = 4 \times 0.5 = 2$$
So one mole of citric acid evolves 2 moles of hydrogen.

options.A: 0.5 is far too small. This is the amount of H2 from just one O-H group, as if citric acid had only one reactive proton. Citric acid actually has four reactive O-H protons.
options.B: 1.5 comes from counting only the three carboxylic acid groups (3 x 0.5 = 1.5) and forgetting the alcohol OH. Sodium is strong enough to react with alcohols as well as carboxylic acids, so the HO-C group must also be included.
options.C: Correct and well done. Three -CO2H groups plus one alcohol -OH gives 4 moles of reactive H per mole of acid. Since 2H gives H2, moles of H2 = 4 / 2 = 2.
options.D: 4 confuses moles of H with moles of H2. There are indeed 4 moles of reactive H atoms, but hydrogen gas is diatomic, so two H atoms make one H2 molecule. You must divide by 2.
